title: Venezuela's Oil Production Push: 3 Energy Stocks to Watch Now - The Globe and Mail
content: Venezuela is reportedly aiming to increase its crude oil production to 2.9 million barrels per day (bpd) over the next decade, per the government’s recently published Plan Venezuela Renace. The target represents a substantial increase from the 1.22 million bpd reported by Venezuela for October 2026. The Orinoco Oil Belt is expected to account for more than half of the country's future production. Venezuela, which holds recoverable crude oil reserves of 300 billion barrels, sees the potential to increase near-term output by up to 1 million bpd through the restoration of existing infrastructure. Further production growth will depend largely on foreign investments and additional capacity development. Venezuela’s ambitious production expansion plan presents significant growth opportunities for international energy companies. The country anticipates oil-sector capital expenditures of $160 billion between 2026 and 2036, with foreign partners expected to contribute $85 billion. Amendments to the Hydrocarbons Law and the easing of U.S. restrictions are expected to encourage foreign participation in Venezuela’s energy sector. Moreover, rising U.S. demand for Venezuelan heavy crude provides a favorable backdrop for production expansion. While financing constraints, sanctions and crude price volatility remain key risks, the targeted production increase presents potential growth opportunities for energy majors like Chevron Corporation CVX, Eni S.p.A. E and Repsol, S.A. REPYY. Chevron has a century-long presence in Venezuela, providing the energy major with extensive operational expertise and established infrastructure. During the third quarter of 2026, CVX expanded its acreage and secured improved fiscal terms, making its Venezuelan operations more profitable and competitive. Its three joint ventures plan to invest $7 billion over the next five years, targeting a doubling of gross oil production to approximately 600,000 barrels per day by 2031. Importantly, the expansion is expected to be self-funded, with combined capital and operating costs below $20 per barrel. Existing infrastructure eliminates the need for major additional infrastructure investments, supporting attractive returns. Chevron also markets 100% of the crude produced by these ventures, with the majority supplied to U.S. refineries, including its Pascagoula and El Segundo facilities. Venezuela’s planned production expansion thus positions CVX to strengthen its upstream earnings, secure additional crude supplies for its refining operations and support long-term free cash flow growth. CVX currently carries a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold). You can see the complete list of today’s Zacks #1 Rank (Strong Buy) stocks here. Eni’s established presence in Venezuela through the Junín-5, Perla and Corocoro fields positions the Italian energy major to capitalize on the country’s production expansion. In September 2026, E secured a new 25-year contractual agreement for the Junín-5 oilfield. Subject to regulatory approval, the first development phase targets gross production of 200,000 barrels per day within 24 months, with full-field development potentially unlocking 1 million barrels per day in the 2030s. Eni and Repsol have jointly committed $2 billion to their Venezuelan operations over the next five years. Eni’s 50% stake in the Cardón IV gas venture provides additional growth opportunities through production expansion and a proposed floating liquefied natural gas (LNG) export facility. Moreover, revised contractual terms give Eni control over Perla’s exports and revenues, facilitating the recovery of outstanding payments. Existing infrastructure and phased investments are expected to limit initial capital requirements, supporting upstream profitability, financial flexibility and long-term cash flow growth. Eni also currently carries a Zacks Rank #3. Repsol is well-positioned to benefit from Venezuela’s oil production recovery through its interests in Petroquiriquire, Petrocarabobo and Cardón IV. The Spanish energy major’s Venezuelan production averaged 72,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in the third quarter of 2026. Since assuming operatorship of Petroquiriquire in April, REPYY has awarded several contracts to increase light crude production. Management aims to increase oil production from its Venezuelan assets by 50% in the near term and triple output within three years. Repsol is also progressing toward securing a new production participation contract for Petrocarabobo, offering substantial heavy crude production growth potential. Its 50% stake in Cardón IV provides exposure to gas production expansion and prospective LNG exports. Additionally, Repsol has monetized three crude oil cargoes received as payment for gas production in 2026, with two more expected by year-end. Higher production and improved payment mechanisms position REPYY to strengthen upstream earnings and cash generation while facilitating the recovery of outstanding receivables. Repsol currently sports a Zacks Rank #1. Venezuela’s renewed efforts to revive its oil and gas industry offer attractive growth prospects for international energy companies with established operations in the country. Improved contractual terms, access to vast hydrocarbon resources and the easing of U.S. restrictions create a favorable investment environment. Chevron, Eni and Repsol are strategically positioned to capitalize on these developments through production expansion, efficient capital deployment and improved cash generation. While political uncertainty, financing challenges and commodity price volatility remain concerns, successful execution of development plans offers significant long-term upside. Investors may benefit from keeping these three energy stocks on their watchlists as Venezuela advances toward its ambitious production target. The AI revolution has already minted millionaires. CVX now wants to focus on assets that have stronger long-term growth potential.In the past six months, Devon’s shares have underperformed the Zacks Oil & Gas- Exploration and Production- United States industry’s growth. In the past six months, Chevron’s shares have gained 15.6%.Should you consider adding DVN to your portfolio only based on weakness in price movements? Let’s delve deeper and find out the factors that can help investors decide whether it is a good entry point to add DVN stock to their portfolio. Devon's expanded U.S. portfolio spans the Permian, Rockies, Anadarko and Marcellus regions, providing diversified exposure to oil, natural gas and natural gas liquids (NGLs). Higher output from newly drilled wells continues to support production growth across its operating areas, while the addition of legacy Coterra Energy assets is contributing to overall production volumes.Devon's planned divestiture of the Eagle Ford assets for $4.2 billion is expected to strengthen its financial flexibility and support shareholder returns. The company anticipates approximately $3.5 billion in proceeds after taxes and effective-date adjustments. The transaction is also expected to reduce its underlying production decline rate and corporate breakeven costs while extending its drilling inventory life, strengthening long-term operational efficiency.Devon remains focused on improving capital efficiency, reducing operating costs and realizing merger-related synergies. In its November 2026 update, the company raised its expected year-end 2026 annualized pre-tax synergy run rate to approximately $350 million from $200 million. DVN also increased its anticipated average 2027 synergies to $700 million from $600 million, reflecting progress in integrating Coterra Energy's operations and streamlining expenses.Devon ended the third quarter of 2026 with $3.4 billion in liquidity, comprising $413 million in cash and an undrawn $3 billion credit facility. Total debt stood at $10.6 billion following repayment of the remaining $750 million term loan, bringing cumulative debt reduction since the Coterra merger to $1.25 billion. With no debt maturities until the second quarter of 2027, Devon aims to reduce gross debt to approximately $9 billion in early 2027, supported by operating cash flows and anticipated Eagle Ford divestiture proceeds. This improved financial position should provide flexibility to fund development activities and shareholder distributions.Devon also employs a disciplined hedging strategy to mitigate commodity price volatility and improve cash flow visibility. title: Can Chevron Build a Lithium Business in the Smackover Formation? - TradingView
content: Chevron Corporation CVX entered the U.S. lithium sector in June 2025, when it announced two leasehold acquisitions in the Smackover Formation in Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas. The company initially put the combined position at about 125,000 net acres and later revised that figure to about 135,000 net acres. Chevron acquired the leases to find out whether it can produce lithium from salty water found deep underground. The company is pursuing lithium mainly for energy storage, including batteries used in electric vehicles and on the power grid. Chevron is assessing the underground resource, testing direct lithium extraction and designing the facilities it would need. The process separates lithium from salty water pumped to the surface, then returns the remaining water to the underground reservoir. That work draws on skills Chevron already uses in its oil and gas business, from assessing reservoirs to drilling wells and handling fluids. The company is also refining its product specifications so it can discuss with potential customers what they need and what the project might eventually be able to supply. Chevron plans to develop the acreage in phases and adjust the pace to market conditions. The company has yet to announce when commercial production might start or how much lithium it aims to produce. Oil and gas production still drives most of Chevron’s earnings, so the near-term question for investors is what the extraction tests reveal about the project’s economics. How much lithium Chevron can recover from the brine, and what it costs to recover it, will help determine whether the acreage can support a profitable business. A U.S. lithium supply chain depends on producers being able to meet battery makers’ quality standards consistently. Producing battery-grade lithium in small batches is an early step. The next test is whether that quality holds as output increases. ExxonMobil Holdings XOM holds brine rights across more than 300,000 net acres in the Smackover Formation. ExxonMobil has produced battery-grade lithium carbonate at its Texas pilot facility using brine from southern Arkansas. ExxonMobil’s preliminary agreement with LG Chem for a potential lithium supply deal is nonbinding. The company aims to produce enough lithium for about one million electric vehicles a year by the first half of the 2030s. Occidental Petroleum OXY is testing direct lithium extraction in California’s Imperial Valley through a joint venture with BHE Renewables. Occidental’s TerraLithium subsidiary and its partner produced battery-grade lithium carbonate from geothermal brine and converted lithium chloride into lithium hydroxide in separate tests. Occidental and its partner expect demonstration operations to continue through 2027 as they assess whether the process is economically viable at commercial scale.
